Control.

Control of your computer and control of your data, as well as control of your personal information. It's a mixture of a tactic to try to remain relevant against the swelling masses of Android and iOS installations, future-proofing the platform (and, if they're lucky, the userbase), and finding a new stream of monetization. And in the end, control of computing.

There are a lot of people who are putting out a ton of text about how Windows 10's model improves a number of things. They are, to a point, correct. In theory, automatic patching is a good thing. In theory, signed bootloaders are a good thing. In theory, encouraging backups to the cloud is a good thing.

Note how many "in theory" caveats there are in that list.

However, look at it on the flipside. With the locked bootloaders they're pushing with Secure Boot, they get to dictate what OS you're using, cutting down sharply on choice. Automatic patching means that whatever code they want runs on your machine and you have no choice in the matter, even if it ends up breaking your system or does things you don't want to do. Look at how Windows 10 PCs help to spread it - they've commandeered your computer for what amounts to a BitTorrent node!

And why are they SO secretive with the data they collect? Why do they prevent you from turning data gathering off off? Why do their patches "accidentally" re-enable it? Why is it SO pervasive? What assurance has Microsoft given that it will NOT somehow end up having this data used against us?

The answers - or rather, LACK of answers - to all of these questions and problems should make one ill at ease in terms of their implications. Especially since, even if the current corporate structure uses everything in the most angelic of ways, that data is likely going to be around for the next few decades and possibly much, much longer. You may draw your last breath before that data is even close to being deleted.

And all of this gives ways for Windows to control its revenue streams, as well as build new ones, particularly the lucrative data collection used by Facebook and Google, among others. However, if taken to its logical conclusion, this gets to a more sinister motive.

Long story short, everybody and their brother is trying to get on Cloud Computing. Ultimately, while it is efficient, dynamic and clever, it ultimately occurs on SOMEONE ELSE'S hardware. And that would be the ultimate coup, both in terms of personal liberty as well as the revenue of Microsoft and its revenue streams. If your computer becomes a dumb terminal, the ultimate vendor lock-in is in effect.

And Windows 10, with its heavily pushed cloud features, is a good beachhead for just that. It takes your computer and tries to make it a node in Microsoft's network for them, and a dumb terminal for you. There are ways to weasel around this to a large extent - for instance, get past Microsoft's attempts to trick you into building a Microsoft account and locking yourself in there - but all things considered, conditions are ripe for things to get a LOT worse, in no small part because they already have by the mere fact that Windows 10 exists.

I'm sure there are other reasons and interpretations, and I might well get hit by a text wall by someone who says how great everything is with Windows 10. I have noticed that these tend to be people with an ulterior motive (not necessarily being shills paid by Microsoft, but, for instance, at least one developer who melted down at the thought of not getting user crash dumps whether or not they want to provide them), and people who are clinging to some level of denial about what can be done with all that data.

And that's why Microsoft is most likely trying to force Windows 10 on people, often by trickery and deception, and trying to force people to take the operating system the way they demand it be taken, even while providing the illusion of choice. They do not want to provide the public with choices for the customer, they want to provide and limit choices to those that will favor Microsoft the most, and use their position to give users little practical choice, since not everyone can move to Linux or a Mac (and many flat-out CAN'T move), and Secure Boot changes may well make that vastly harder. They have seen the writing on the wall, so they are trying to do it their way - and grab every bit of control and potentially useful information that they can. In many ways they have bet the company on this - while I doubt they'll disintegrate if it fails, they've seen how IBM went from giant to a struggling shadow of its former self in the last couple decades, and are rather desparate not to go down that hole. That, I can't fault them for. But their explicit limitation of choice, their assertion of sovereignty over personal property, their dictation from on high regardless of the consequences, charging extra just to have some limited additional control of your computer (e.g. Win 10 Pro)... things like this, I most definitely can and do fault them for.

Also, it is worth noting that Windows 10 is ALREADY being sold for cash. They're making conventional revenue on it, and I'd be flabbergasted if they aren't charging the Royalty OEMs at the very least. The "free upgrade" only applies to existing copies.
